title: May this repair be deducted from the security deposit, and for how much?

source.quote: The deductions for repairs and cleaning together do not exceed one hundred twenty-five dollars ($125).

children.statement: The deposit secures a rental agreement for residential property used as the tenant's dwelling.

source.quote: This section applies to security for a rental agreement for residential property that is used as the dwelling of the tenant.

children.statement: The money held was imposed at the beginning of the tenancy (or as advance rent) and is not a screening fee under Section 1950.6.

source.quote: “security” means any payment, fee, deposit, or charge, including, but not limited to, any payment, fee, deposit, or charge, except as provided in Section 1950.6, that is imposed at the beginning of the tenancy to be used to reimburse the landlord for costs associated with processing a new tenant or that is imposed as an advance payment of rent, used or to be used for any purpose

children.statement: The line pays for repairing damage to the premises.

source.quote: The repair of damages to the premises, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, caused by the tenant or by a guest or licensee of the tenant.

children.statement: The damage was caused by the tenant or by a guest or licensee of the tenant.

question.wording: Do the move-out observations and the tenancy record show that this damage was caused by the tenant, a member of the household, or a guest or licensee of the tenant during the tenancy, rather than by the landlord, a vendor, a previous occupant, or an outside event such as a leak or storm?

source.quote: The repair of damages to the premises, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, caused by the tenant or by a guest or licensee of the tenant.

children.statement: The damage did not exist before the tenancy began.

question.wording: Comparing the move-in record and photographs with the move-out observations, was this damage absent at the start of the tenancy?

source.quote: The landlord shall not assert a claim against the tenant or the security for damages to the premises or any defective conditions that preexisted the tenancy

children.statement: The damage resulted from an accident, misuse, abuse or neglect, not from normal use or aging.

question.wording: Does the evidence show that this condition resulted from an accident, misuse, abuse or neglect, rather than from normal everyday use or the aging of the item?

basis.quote: Normal wear and tear includes simple wearing down of carpet and drapes because of normal use or aging and includes moderate dirt or spotting.

source.quote: for ordinary wear and tear or the effects thereof, whether the wear and tear preexisted the tenancy or occurred during the tenancy

children.statement: The damage is more extensive than the deterioration normal use would produce over this tenancy.

question.wording: Is this condition more extensive than the deterioration normal use would cause over a tenancy of this length (for example a large rip, an indelible stain, many holes needing patching, or a large gouge, rather than simple wearing, moderate dirt or spotting, or minor marks or nicks)?

basis.quote: In contrast, large rips or indelible stains justify a deduction from the tenant’s security deposit for repairing the carpet or drapes or replacing them if that is reasonably necessary.
Generally, minor marks or nicks in walls are the landlord’s responsibility as normal wear and tear (for example, worn paint caused by a sofa against the wall).

source.quote: The repair of damages to the premises, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear, caused by the tenant or by a guest or licensee of the tenant.

children.statement: The damage is not the accumulated effect of ordinary wear over this or earlier tenancies.

question.wording: Is this condition something other than the accumulated effect of ordinary wear over this and earlier tenancies (such as gradual fading, traffic wear, or build-up from years of use)?

source.quote: or for the cumulative effects of ordinary wear and tear occurring during any one or more tenancies.

children.statement: The damaged item still had useful life remaining when the tenancy ended, under the company schedule.

source.quote: or for the cumulative effects of ordinary wear and tear occurring during any one or more tenancies.

children.statement: The initial-inspection itemized statement does not bar this deduction.

source.quote: the landlord shall not use the security for deductions for repairs or cleanings that are not identified in the itemized statement described in paragraph (2).

children.statement: The work restores the premises to their condition at the start of the tenancy and does not improve them.

question.wording: Does the work charged restore this item to its condition at the start of the tenancy, without upgrading it (for example a better material, a larger scope, or a replacement where a repair would restore it)?

basis.quote: It is the intent of the Legislature, in enacting this measure, to ensure that landlords do not subsidize improvements to their rental properties with a former tenant’s security deposit.

source.quote: Claims against the tenant or the security for materials or supplies and for work performed by a contractor, the landlord, or the landlord’s employee shall be limited to a reasonable amount necessary to restore the premises back to the condition it was in at the inception of the tenancy, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear.

children.statement: The cost charged is no more than a reasonable amount for the work needed to restore the item.

question.wording: Is the cost charged for this work (the vendor invoice, or the hours and hourly rate for in-house work, plus materials) no more than a reasonable amount for the work needed, judged against the company rate schedule and any other quotes obtained?

source.quote: Claims against the tenant or the security for materials or supplies and for work performed by a contractor, the landlord, or the landlord’s employee shall be limited to a reasonable amount necessary to restore the premises back to the condition it was in at the inception of the tenancy, exclusive of ordinary wear and tear.

children.statement: The statement carries the work documents: for in-house work a description with time spent and a reasonable hourly rate; for vendor work the bill, invoice or receipt with the vendor's name, address and telephone; for materials a bill, invoice, receipt or vendor price list.

source.quote: The landlord shall also include, along with and at the same time the itemized statement is sent, copies of documents showing charges incurred and deducted by the landlord to repair or clean the premises, as follows:

children.statement: The statement provides the subdivision (g) photographs for this repair and a written explanation of its cost.

source.quote: If a deduction is made for repairs or cleanings allowed by this section, the landlord shall provide photographs taken pursuant to subdivision (g), along with a written explanation of the cost of the allowable repairs or cleanings, as described in subparagraphs (A) to (C), inclusive.

children.statement: Repair and cleaning deductions on the statement together do not exceed $125.

source.quote: The deductions for repairs and cleaning together do not exceed one hundred twenty-five dollars ($125).

children.statement: The tenant signed a waiver of the documentation rights at or after a termination notice, or no earlier than 60 days before a fixed term expires.

source.quote: The waiver shall only be effective if it is signed by the tenant at the same time or after a notice to terminate a tenancy under Section 1946 or 1946.1 has been given, a notice under Section 1161 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been given, or no earlier than 60 calendar days prior to the expiration of a fixed-term lease.

children.statement: The waiver substantially includes the text of Civil Code section 1950.5(h)(2).

question.wording: Does the signed waiver substantially include the text of Civil Code section 1950.5(h)(2), the paragraph requiring copies of work documents, invoices and photographs with the statement?

source.quote: The waiver shall substantially include the text of paragraph (2).

children.statement: The deduction is a good-faith estimate made under subdivision (h)(3).

source.quote: the landlord may deduct the amount of a good faith estimate of the charges that will be incurred and provide that estimate with the itemized statement.

effects.statement: The repair may be deducted at the reasonable cost times the tenant's share under the company schedule; a good-faith estimate stands in for the cost where subdivision (h)(3) applies.

source.quote: the landlord may claim of the security only those amounts as are reasonably necessary for the purposes specified in subdivision (b).

effects.statement: The repair may not be deducted from the security.
